中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

Four Corners

Four Corners examines the scale of Canberra's revolving door, where former government officials turn to lobbying or accept lucrative jobs representing private interests.

PLAYERS: How are you? How are you?

MARK WILLACY, REPORTER: It's a crisp Canberra morning…and MPs and staffers are gathering at a field in the shadow of parliament house for a friendly hit out. Today's football match has been organised by the Parliament Sports Club.

ORGANISER: hello can I get everyone's attention please?

DAVID POCOCK, INDEPENDENT SENATOR: Parliamentary Sports Club is an organisation that essentially facilitates sport in the mornings. It's a great way to get to know your colleagues. Staff turn up, people who work at Parliament House turn up.

ORGANISER: anyone this morning that stands out, you could be on the plane to America, so no pressure

MARK WILLACY: To Wallabies rugby union captain turned Senator David Pocock, this morning's match is a welcome antidote to the claustrophobia of the chamber that awaits. But what he doesn't know — at least at this point — is that the privately-owned Parliament Sports Club is about more than sport.

DAVID POCOCK: Turns out, and, you know, myself and many of my colleagues didn't know this, they were essentially being sponsored by a whole bunch of companies, industry groups, including the gambling lobby. And so, the gambling lobby were paying for access to events.

DR MONIQUE RYAN, INDEPENDENT MP: It turned out it was also a way for lobbyists to access politicians when we're off guard in the early morning and basically to cozy up to them.

MARK WILLACY: Watching from the sidelines this morning is the most powerful sports betting lobbyist in the country…the CEO of Responsible Wagering Australia, Kai Cantwell.

REV. TIM COSTELLO, ALLIANCE FOR GAMBLING REFORM: Oh, their access is extraordinary. They're all over every politician. And they never miss a trick.

MARK WILLACY: David Pocock has taken a hard line against one of the gambling industry's most potent weapons — sports betting advertising…he wants it sin-binned from our screens. So, the involvement of Responsible Wagering Australia in the Parliament Sports Club - as well as others like alcohol and fossil fuel companies - meant — to him — that a line had been crossed.

DAVID POCOCK: Because of the way the Parliamentary Sports Club was set up and operating, they had advice that they had to list themselves as a lobbying organisation on the lobbyist register. The prime minister is essentially like the patron of the sports club. And so, you had the prime minister who's essentially the patron of a lobbying firm for all intents and purposes if you go by the lobbying register.

MARK WILLACY: The Parliamentary Sports Club turned out to be a registered lobbying firm?

DAVID POCOCK: It did. And when I raised concerns about this, I was kicked out of the club. Got an angry phone call saying, 'Mate, you're, you know, you're causing trouble. You're out'.

ANDY TURNBULL: Football was the winner, that's time now, all over

MARK WILLACY: The Sports Club CEO Andy Turnbull declined Four Corners' interview request but he told us corporate money was used to hold fixtures and dinners and for running costs and that club members were aware of this corporate support.

MARK WILLACY: You're a former Wallabies captain. Is this the first team you've ever been kicked out of?

DAVID POCOCK: Yeah, I think it probably is, yeah

MARK WILLACY: The Parliament Sports Club removed itself from the lobbyist register just a few days after David Pocock was kicked out

DAVID POCOCK: I think the Parliamentary Sports Club debacle highlights just how normalised it is that for many in there, it's just the status quo. People that are part of industries pay for access. They lobby hard, they get privileged access. And that's just how things work in this place.

MARK WILLACY: Four Corners has examined lobbying registers, ministerial diaries and political donations to investigate who gets access to Australia's decision makers … and how little the public is told about it.

SAFFRON ZOMER, AUSTRALIAN DEMOCRACY NETWORK: Australians do really value our democracy. And we want it to be fair. And broken lobbying system makes our democracy work unfairly in the interest of the powerful few and not in the best interest of everyone else.

MARK WILLACY: Lobbying has been part of the Australian political landscape for decades…but critics say that never before has there been so many lobbyists with so much access to decision-makers and so much influence over policy. Inside the people's house, hundreds of unelected representatives have privileged access to those who make the country's laws.

DR MONIQUE RYAN: You can spot lobbyists in the wild by their orange passes. So you have to have a pass which is sponsored by a member of parliament. Those lobbyists can knock on the door and have free access to parliamentarians, when other people have got very valid concerns or complaints who would like to talk to us are denied that opportunity.

MARK WILLACY: Four of the country's top lobbying firms agreed to talk to Four Corners and to reveal how they operate.

MARK WILLACY: It's been extremely rare for lobbyists to come on television, particularly Four Corners, and explain how it all works. Why did you decide to do that?

CHRISTOPHER PYNE, CHAIRMAN, PYNE & PARTNERS: Well, I don't want people to think that lobbyists are like nocturnal creatures who only come out in the dark and don't want anyone to notice them. There's nothing wrong with advocating on behalf of clients to government.

SIMON BANKS, CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER HAWKER BRITTON: There are broadly three types of lobbyists. The first, like me, is a third-party lobbyist. We're effectively contracted in by companies and organisations to assist them with their government relations need and we're required to register under the Commonwealth government's lobbyist register.

MATTHEW HARRIS, CHIEF EXECUTIVE OFFICER BARTON DEAKIN: The second type of lobbyists are in-house lobbyists who work on behalf of large corporations who are representing the interests of that particular business. They don't have to disclose that they are lobbying, but they have access to Parliament House and are advocating on behalf of the interests of their employer.

EAMONN FITZPATRICK, MANAGING DIRECTOR FITZPATRICK & CO: The third type of lobbyist is the industry association lobbyist. They might work for a business council; they might work for a trade association. Either way, they do exactly the same sort of work as a third-party lobbyist, but they're exempt from having to register under the Federal Lobbying Code.

DAVID POCOCK: Lobbying is not the problem. It's just the total lack of transparency.

MARK WILLACY: You're outnumbered, aren't you?

DR MONIQUE RYAN: We are. We're surrounded.

EAMONN FITZPATRICK: Australian democracy doesn't need a lobbyist at all, but our economy does absolutely.

MARK WILLACY: Eamonn Fitzpatrick runs lobbying firm — Fitzpatrick & Co Advisory.

Previously he was a senior adviser to Prime Ministers Kevin Rudd and Julia Gillard.

EAMONN FITZPATRICK: I think lobbyists provide a very useful service

SIMON BANKS: Government is big and it is complex. So, employing a lobbyist helps you navigate through those parts.

MARK WILLACY: Simon Banks leads Australia's biggest lobbying firm…the Labor-aligned Hawker Britton… He served as chief of staff to Labor leaders Simon Crean and Kevin Rudd.

MARK WILLACY: Is it a lucrative industry to be in?

SIMON BANKS: Look it's well paid. I don't think anyone would suggest to you that it's not. There's certainly I guess a premium for the service.

MATTHEW HARRIS: I would argue the currency of a good lobbyist is the expertise we provide, not the access.

MARK WILLACY: Matthew Harris is the CEO of Barton Deakin…a Liberal and National Party-aligned lobbying firm. He's a former Victorian State Director of the National Party.

MARK WILLACY: Why have you agreed to talk to Four Corners about lobbying and what you do?

MATTHEW HARRIS: I'm really proud of what we do, not just at Barton Deakin, but also across the industry and I think we play a really important role in Australia's future.

CHRISTOPHER PYNE: So, having been in the House of Representatives for 26 years and been involved in sifting through many ideas and having your own ideas, lobbying is really an extension of what I did before, which is talking to people about their ideas.

MARK WILLACY: Christopher Pyne is the chairman of Pyne & Partners… He served as Australia's Defence Minister and Leader of the House of Representatives. A renowned political operative, he cultivated countless relationships across the aisle during his two-and-a-half decades in parliament.

CHRISDTOPHER PYNE ARCHIVE: I'm a fixer, I fixed it

CHRISTOPHER PYNE: So, I always played the ball, not the person. And I'm not an extremist, of course. I'm sort of a smaller liberal, centre right liberal type. So, there's no particular reason to hate me.

MARK WILLACY: Having those relationships across the aisle though, it must be good for business?

CHRISTOPHER PYNE: it's very good for business. Yeah.

MARK WILLACY: As third-party operators, these four lobbying leaders have to register themselves, their firms, and their clients with state and federal governments. But they say those rules don't apply to the hordes of in-house lobbyists who work directly for companies and big corporations…and who also have a pass giving them valuable access to parliament.

DAVID POCOCK: Actually, the vast majority of lobbyists aren't on the register because they don't work for a lobbying firm. They are lobbying on behalf of their company, you know? Qantas government relations, not a lobbyist. It's their job to lobby.

MARK WILLACY: How does the Commonwealth rank when it comes to lobbying rules compared to the states and territories?

SAFFRON ZOMER: Dead last. The whole lobbying system at the moment is broken. So, Australians just can't know who's trying to influence government decisions, who they're meeting with, when they meet. That's all behind closed doors.

MARK WILLACY: Even some lobbyists believe the rules need a shake up.

EAMONN FITZPATRICK: The rules need to change. They need to be wider and broader and more so than ever, you know? More transparent. Yeah, 100%. We need to be more transparent. Transparency means we get rid of the shonks.

SIMON BANKS: So that's why I say those sort of rules, of course they should apply to someone like me, but anyone else who's performing that role in government relations, well, it should apply to them too. And if you breach those rules, well, there should be consequences for it no matter who you are.

MARK WILLACY: Under new reforms, in-house lobbyists now need two sponsors to get a parliamentary pass…and their details will be published on a website…but critics say the system is still not good enough.

DAVID POCOCK: It's embarrassingly lax. Then there's total lack of transparency as to who has access to the building. We've got this system where, and this, this blew my mind after being elected. As a parliamentarian, you can give out an unlimited number of sponsored passes to anyone really.

MARK WILLACY: But critics say the flaws in the system extend well beyond who gets a parliamentary pass. It goes back further, to where many of these lobbyists come from…and their links to those in power.

MARK WILLACY: What is the revolving door and why is it a problem?

SAFFRON ZOMER: So, the revolving door describes the phenomenon where people leave political roles and then become lobbyists who are paid to influence the decisions that their former colleagues make on public interest matters. It's a problem because it's not fair. It's not meant to be a marketplace where access and influence get bought and sold.

MARK WILLACY: The revolving door has long spun hard and fast in Australian politics…a gateway for ministers, MPs and senior advisers to move into lucrative positions in private lobbying firms or in industry…often in sectors they once regulated or oversaw. There is nothing illegal about it. But in their private sector careers, they are potentially able to leverage their connections to gain privileged access…and they can draw on their insider knowledge to help the commercial interests they represent.

DAVID POCOCK: It's the system that sucks. It's the system that is selling all of us out. And you've got dozens of examples of ministers that have gone on to accept pretty plum jobs in companies, in industries, set up lobbying firms, and really milk the system.

MARK WILLACY: Even some lobbyists acknowledge that the revolving door is a lucrative transition that could trigger serious conflicts of interest.

SIMON BANKS: Clearly there are circumstances where people could walk out of a job today. They can hold very valuable information about government decisions and processes, and they should not be able to commercialise those activities. That is government, very valuable government information that needs to be protected and you need good processes to prevent that from happening.

MARK WILLACY: One of those processes is spelled out in the official Federal Lobbying Code of Conduct and it involves the so-called cooling off period. For ministers its supposed to be 18 months, for senior advisers and public servants it's a year before they can lobby in areas the once worked in.

CHRISTOPHER PYNE: It's a pretty simple rule, you know, if you've been a minister…for 18 months after you leave politics you cant approach or talk to the previous people that you dealt with in that department certainly about anything to do with work, I mean you can wish them happy birthday, but you're not allowed to talk to them about work.

MARK WILLACY: To your knowledge are the cooling off periods even policed?

DR MONIQUE RYAN: I don't believe that the cooling off periods are ever policed. I have not seen any evidence of that.

DAVID SHOEBRIDGE, SENATOR, AUSTRALIAN GREENS: When we raise this with the government, we raise this with departments we get told nothing to see here, nothing to see.

MARK WILLACY: Is it monetising your public service?

EAMONN FITZPATRICK: Everything gets monetised, Mark. Everything. That's just the modern world.

MARK WILLACY: What do you say to the critics who say, 'Well, you're just monetising your public service.' What's your riposte to that?

CHRISTOPHER PYNE: Well, see, I had a quarter of a century in politics. So, I have a wealth of experience of how government works, how opposition works, how politics works. So to me, it would be crazy not to tap into that experience in that lifetime of learning about the political system.

DR MONIQUE RYAN: I mean, Christopher's a charming individual. He's the perfect person to be. He's charming and smart. He could sell tea to China. You know, he's going to be a fantastic lobbyist. If I was a lobbying company, I would glum onto him too, because he's going to do a great job. But, you know, he has inside knowledge that he has gained from decades in parliament and years as a defence minister, which he has taken into the defence industry.

MARK WILLACY: You've been operating for a few years now. How, how's business going?

CHRISTOPHER PYNE: We're number one in defence, number two in infrastructure and construction. Business is good. I'm very happy.

MARK WILLACY: Is it a lucrative industry?

CHRISTOPHER PYNE: Well, is it a lucrative. Yes, it's a profitable industry, otherwise you wouldn't be in business.

MARK WILLACY: For lobbying firms, defence is a bonanza…with their clients keen to cash in on the 368-billion-dollar AUKUS deal between Australia, the US and the UK.

DAVID SHOEBRIDGE: there are entire careers, entire harborside mansions, new consulting contracts. Like this is the feast of all feasts.

CHRISTOPHER PYNE: Obviously, I mean, it's not a secret to say there's $368 billion being spent on AUKUS over the lifetime of the agreement. And therefore, there's a lot of businesses, UK, US, Australian, who want to be part of that story. So AUKUS is important to us, and the defence industry is important to us, but it's heavily scrutinised. It's hard to work out how much more scrutiny you could have because.

MARK WILLACY: So, it's not a free for all?

CHRISTOPHER PYNE: Definitely not. I mean it certainly is not a free for all.

MARK WILLACY: This year, Pyne and Partners paid for travel and accommodation for senior Labor Senator Deborah O'Neill to travel to Washington to participate in the firm's five-thousand dollar-a-head annual AUKUS conference…. we asked the senator about her trip … she said it was within the rules and that she declared it.

DAVID SHOEBRIDGE: Literally, he pays for a politician who's inside the government to come across and schmooze with his $5,000 a pop clientele and future clientele and potential clientele over to Washington. And it's a demonstration for them that, look at this bloke, he's got an inside into government. Look, he's got a senator. He brought a senator over.

MARK WILLACY: The Labor senator wasn't even close to the highest-ranking figure to speak at the Pyne and Partners' AUKUS event in Washington…

DAVID SHOEBRIDGE: (Senate Estimates, 3 June 2026): Were you aware that people were paying $4,950 to a lobbyist firm to attend your speech?

VICE ADM. MARK HAMMOND, CHIEF OF NAVY (3 June 2026): Vice Admiral Mark Hammond Chief of Navy. The short answer is no. The invitation to speak at that event and other activities—I think I had seven speaking engagements whilst I conducted that trip—that invitation came in late last year. It was referred to the minister's office.

MARK WILLACY: Christopher Pyne says it's a natural fit for the incoming chief of defence to speak at an event focussing on AUKUS.

CHRISTOPHER PYNE: The other criticism that people always get is that they sit in an ivory tower in Russell Hill or Capitol Hill and never talk to anyone. So, then opportunities are created by people like me for them to get out and sell their message and also to hear from people about how it's going. And then they get criticized for doing that. So, you know, you can't have it both ways, although people do like to.

MARK WILLACY: While Pyne and Partners is number one in defence, it also has dozens of clients from other industries.

MARK WILLACY: How often do you get the outcome? You know, is it often you don't get the outcome?

CHRISTOPHER PYNE: When you win, obviously, you tell everybody about it. When you don't win, you sort of hope that no one's noticed. So, I mean, I wouldn't know what the percentage of outcomes is, but, you know, business is business. You have a go and you see if you get there or not.

MARK WILLACY: Christopher Pyne is not the only other former defence or defence industry minister to pivot to lobbying or a private sector firm. Liberal David Johnston is on the advisory board of big lobbying company TG Public Affairs…as is former Labor defence minister Kim Beazley. Joel Fitzgibbon who also headed the defence portfolio for Labor is a special counsel to lobbyist CMAX Advisory. While former Labor Defence Materiel minister Mike Kelly became Australian president of the controversial US software and intelligence company Palantir.

MAJOR-GENERAL JEREMY KING (October, 2024): Welcome to Holsworthy Barracks. I hope you saw an impressive display of Army's newest aircraft; the UH-60 Mike Black Hawk this morning.

MARK WILLACY: it's not just former ministers who walk through the revolving door…

DAVID SHOEBRIDGE: Jeremy King was one of the most senior members inside the Army, a Major General, and responsible for a series of critical procurement decisions and most notably getting a US weapon system called the Black Hawk helicopter.

MARK WILLACY: Major General King had a key role in the Army's 2023 decision to replace the Taipan helicopter with 40 Black Hawks built by the world's largest defence company — Lockheed Martin…in a two-point-eight-billion-dollar deal.

MARK WILLACY: And where is Jeremy King now?

DAVID SHOEBRIDGE: Well, he's running Lockheed Martin Australia, of course. And you know, when we were checking the data, there, there, there wasn't even a week between walking out of defence taking the most senior position in Lockheed Martin, Australia.

MARK WILLACY: I think it was January five this year he leaves the military. January 12, a week later, he's appointed or announced as the new CEO of Lockheed Martin, Australia, New Zealand.

DAVID SHOEBRIDGE: They can literally walk out of defence one day and walk into an arms manufacturer, a defence consultant, a lobby group the next.

MARK WILLACY: In a statement to Four Corners, Lockheed Martin said it had instituted rigorous conflict of interest safeguards that isolate Jeremy King from programs connected to his defence service.

MARK WILLACY: Another multi-billion-dollar industry that's benefited from the revolving door has been gambling. According to Transparency International, gambling companies hire more federal lobbying firms than any other harmful industry, twice as many as alcohol… and there's one sports betting lobbyist that is particularly powerful

DR MONIQUE RYAN: Responsible Wagering Australia is the lobbying group on behalf of the gambling industry. My understanding is that it takes no prisoners in its pursuit of the best interests of the gambling industry in Parliament House.

MARK WILLACY: Kai Cantwell is regarded as one of the most effective lobbyists…he's a regular presence in Parliament House, although neither he nor Responsible Wagering Australia are required to be on the federal lobbyist register because RWA is an industry association.

REV. TIM COSTELLO: Kai Cantwell effectively lives at Aussies, which is the cafe inside Parliament House where you meet all the ministers, all the journalists. He set up permanent camp there. So, he's very effective.

DAVD POCOCK: He's forever setting up shop in the break rooms, which are meant to be for staff to actually go and have a lunch break and, you know, use a microwave. He's in there doing Zoom calls. Like, clearly camps out at Parliament House and has a lot of access.

MARK WILLACY: David Pocock's office says it has twice reported Kai Cantwell to the Senate's Usher of the Black Rod for using the staff break rooms to hold video meetings. The Responsible Wagering Australia boss declined our requests for an interview. In an interview with Four Corners last year it was put to the gambling lobbyist that he was regularly knocking on MPs' doors.

KAI CANTWELL (September 2025): I wouldn't say that. I wouldn't characterize it as that as all. I think it would be an intrusion to just go and bang down doors.

MARK WILLACY: There is one door Kai Cantwell is familiar with…the revolving door…

He moved to Responsible Wagering Australia — which represents major gambling companies like Sportsbet and Bet365 — after working as chief of staff to then social services minister Anne Ruston.

DR MONIQUE RYAN: He's helped frame laws to reduce gambling harm. And then he's jumped the fence and he's working for the gambling industry. You have to wonder, at what point did he start to have conversations with the gambling industry about taking up that role?

MARK WILLACY: Kai Cantwell is by no means the only political operative to pass through the revolving door into the gambling lobby or wagering companies. Just a few months after Labor senator and former senior minister Stephen Conroy quit parliament, he took up the position RWA's executive director. And the current chairman of RWA is former longstanding liberal cabinet minister Nick Minchin. Under the federal rules, RWA despite representing some of the biggest gambling players in the country and scoring meetings with state and federal ministers — is not regarded as a lobbying group.

DR MONIQUE RYAN: Well, it's an organization which seeks to change the behaviour of government by meeting with politicians and changing the way that we behave or the decisions that we make. So yes, it's, it's clearly a lobbying group.

MARK WILLACY: In a statement, Responsible Wagering Australia said it complies with all applicable laws, disclosure requirements and parliamentary protocols…and rejects any suggestion its conduct has been improper. The limits of the register matter because the gambling industry has been lobbying during one of the most important policy contests it has faced.

SIMON KENNEDY, LIBERAL MP: just on the gambling 'legge", is that all it is

MARK WILLACY: Simon Kennedy is a federal Liberal MP and the co-chair of the parliamentary friends of gambling harm minimisation

SIMON KENNEDY: This is a country that already has the worst gambling problems in the world, and they've crumpled to the gambling lobby.

MARK WILLACY: A report by the late Labor MP Peta Murphy recommended a complete online gambling advertising blackout, a national regulator, and a ban on inducements. But after a fightback by the gambling lobby, critics say the Albanese government put up a watered-down bill.

SIMON KENNEDY: I want our politicians to be strong enough to stand up to lobbyists. And whether that's the prime minister with the gambling lobbyists, we need our politicians to be acting in the national interest and for everyday Australians, not being the sound pieces from lobbyists and their megaphones.

KATE SESELJA, GAMBLING REFORM ADVOCATE: I almost became one of the gambling related suicides that no one talks about.

MARK WILLACY: Kate Seselja almost lost everything to poker machines…she wants the government to stand up to an industry she says destroys lives.

KATE SESELJA: There was part of me that really, really broke when I realized that my wellbeing as a citizen of Australia was not prioritised from a public health perspective when it comes to gambling harm. That in fact, I was human collateral damage of a tax revenue stream and industry profits.

MARK WILLACY: Labor MP and veteran paediatrician Mike Freelander represents the seat of Macarthur in western Sydney…a community he says has been ravaged by gambling addiction.

DR MIKE FREELANDER, LABOR MP: We see people involved in family breakdown, in family violence, people losing houses.

MARK WILLACY: Four Corners spoke to Mike Freelander in July as the government was trying to get support for its gambling reforms. He wanted the prime minister to take on the gambling industry and its lobbying arm.

DR MIKE FREELANDER: The Prime Minister is very worried about making enemies of very powerful groups. And I think we saw that years ago when we tried to reign in the clubs and pubs, around, you know, poker machines and things. And I understand in some way why he's reticent to take stronger action.

MARK WILLACY: Because this is a very powerful lobby, isn't it?

DR MIKE FREELANDER: Oh, it's unbelievably powerful.

MARK WILLACY: So, the prime minister is obviously cognisant that if he pushes too hard, he's going to have some powerful enemies there.

DR MIKE FREELANDER: Yeah, yeah. Well, you, you know, they're powerful enemies to make. And, um, you know, his, his political judgment's been pretty good so far. I've got to give him credit for that. Certainly, speaking for my community, they would love us to be stronger.

MARK WILLACY: Who do you really want a meeting with? Who would you like to talk to?

KATE SESELJA: I really want to sit down with the PM and have him tell me to my face that he's getting the balance right.

MARK WILLACY: Kate Seselja now works free-of-charge advocating for those who've suffered gambling harm. Like Kai Cantwell, she has a parliamentary pass but she's not getting the meetings she wants.

KATE SESELJA: We have nowhere near the level of access that gambling companies and these industries that feed off gambling interests have as way of access to politicians.

MARK WILLACY: Recently Kate Seselja found herself sitting close to Kai Cantwell at the parliament house cafe when she got a phone call from the distressed father of a young man.

KATE SESELJA, GAMBLING REFORM ADVOCATE: He just discovered that his son was $150,000 in debt from sports betting. And he'd gone so far as pawning he and his wife's rings to try and win back that money. And I'm listening to this man on the worst day of his life talk to me about his 24-year-old son. And I'm filled with rage that a metre away, the man who is paid to protect this industry was right there. And I wanted to just hand him the phone and go, "Kai, you deal with this".

MARK WILLACY: David Pocock says the gambling lobby has won the battle to sway the prime minister…for now.

DAVID POCOCK: This a PM that is captured by the gambling lobby, by the sports, by the broadcasters. So it's tragic and..

MARK WILLACY: The gambling lobby has been very effective.

DAVID POCOCK: Incredibly effective. Yeah. They've, they've won this one because they got to the prime minister.

MARK WILLACY: It's Parliament's annual night of nights the Midwinter Ball. To some, it's an occasion to relax and have a few drinks and an opportunity to rub shoulders with those who shape policy. Among the guests tonight, Kai Cantwell. Also in his finery tonight is Labor MP Dan Repacholi. He's Australia's first special envoy for men's health…he's spoken passionately in the parliament about the devastation caused by gambling.

DAN REPACHOLI IN PARLIAMENT (29 October 2025): For some blokes it leads to something much darker. It leads to stress, shame, financial trouble, and broken relationships. It can push people to breaking point and tear families apart.

MARK WILLACY: While warning of the damage caused by gambling, Dan Repacholi is happy to accept the industry's hospitality. Tonight, the Special Envoy for Men's Health who warns about the evils of gambling is a guest at a table sponsored by Sportsbet.

DAVID POCOCK: I think it's a terrible look. Terrible, terrible look.

MARK WILLACY: Would you accept hospitality from Sportsbet?

DR MIKE FREELANDER: Uh, I wouldn't.

DR MONIQUE RYAN: I thought it was actually a failure of judgment by, by Dan. He's a nice person. He made a really bad call there.

MARK WILLACY: Four Corners caught up with the Special Envoy for Men's Health…but he wasn't keen to chat.

MARK WILLACY: Can I grab you for a second?

DAN REPACHOLI: I got to get back on the conference floor.

MARK WILLACY: It's just a quick question. You've spoken very passionately in the parliament about the impact of men's health, uh, on men's health about gaming. I'm…

DAN REPACHOLI: got to get back into the conference floor. I don't have time to have a chat now, but it's. It's been a good conference here. It's been a good conference here.

MARK WILLACY: It's a pretty easy question…

DAN REPACHOLI: I'm going to have a conversation in there and I'm going to go in and do what I'm doing on my job there in the, conference floor.

MARK WILLACY: Okay then.

MARK WILLACY: In a written statement, Dan Repacholi said he had made all appropriate declarations, including about the Midwinter Ball.

KAI CANTWELL AT SENATE INQUIRY: Kai Cantwell CEO Responsible Wagering Australia

MARK WILLACY: With the Greens and the crossbench initiating a Senate grilling of the sports bet industry, and the opposition unwilling to back his bill, Anthony Albanese was finally forced to give ground last week. Offering a new opt-out scheme for online gambling advertising and a tighter rein on wagering inducements. While it's enough to get the opposition onboard…and his bill through…critics say the gambling lobby is still the winner.

REV TIM COSTELLO: They go on grooming our kids. We have more suicides. We have more domestic violence. We have more crime. They win because this bill isn't good enough.

MARK WILLACY: In trying to get a handle on just how much access the gambling lobby gets, Four Corners analysed the publicly available ministerial diaries from the states and territories. One of the most transparent states is Queensland…and that's where Kai Cantwell appears to have been busiest. On a single day — in August last year — the Responsible Wagering Australia boss met with seven LNP government ministers, including the premier. But what our analysis doesn't — and can't - show is what meetings took place at the federal level because Commonwealth ministerial diaries are not published.

DR MONIQUE RYAN: Ministers do not want us to know who they're meeting with, where, when, and why. And that's because I think if we had that transparency, they'd be asked some pretty uncomfortable questions.

MARK WILLACY: Even some lobbyists have no problem if their meetings with ministers are made public…

SIMON BANKS: I'm perfectly comfortable if ministers want to release their diaries and say who they met with, what were they met with them about. I actually think, what's the thing you're trying to protect? It's integrity of government.

MARK WILLACY: Other lobbyists, like former federal minister Christopher Pyne, oppose releasing ministerial diaries.

CHRISTOPHER PYNE: No, I think it's a mad idea. What do they think the ministers are doing? Let's see. What do these so-called advocates, what do they think the ministers are putting in their diaries that they're going to be revealed, that are going suddenly, what, be a smoking gun?

MARK WILLACY: If access is the currency of lobbying, Konrad Benjamin knows what it's like to be flat broke. Lobbyists have been a feature of the political landscape for decades, but their numbers have never been greater and, according to some critics, neither has their access and influence.

Next week on Four Corners reporter Mark Willacy investigates the opaque business of political lobbyists — where they go, who they meet and what they want.

In Access All Areas, four of the country's top lobbyists — Simon Banks (Hawker Britton), Christopher Pyne (Pyne & Partners), Eamonn Fitzpatrick (Fitzpatrick & Co Advisory) and Matthew Harris (Barton Deakin) — reveal how they operate and why they believe lobbying makes the process of governing more effective. But advocates for stronger oversight and regulation, including some politicians, say the system that is meant to guard against undue influence is broken and vested interests are winning.

Set against the backdrop of the Albanese government's recent efforts to pass its gambling reforms package, the program interrogates the lack of transparency around lobbying activities, which types of lobbyists are more regulated and scrutinised than others, and the 'revolving door' between politics and private enterprise.

And as Four Corners discovered, blatant pay for access schemes are also alive and well in our political system, with lobbyists using them to get "face time" with ministers. So how much do they pay? Who do they get to lobby? And who are the winners?

As the lobbying industry increases in size and sway and faith in politicians wanes, critics say it's time for an effective and functional lobbying regime.

Four Corners: Access All Areas is reported by Mark Willacy and goes to air Monday, August 24 at 8:30pm on ABC TV and ABC iview.
